newsitem.title: UK: London exchange declines comment on AIM censures.
newsitem.headline: London exchange declines comment on AIM censures.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange on Wednesday declined to comment on press speculation about the identities of brokers that may face disciplinary action following a performance review of the Alternative Investment Market (AIM).
"It is not our policy to comment about press rumours," an LSE spokeswoman told Reuters.

The Financial Times newspaper reported on Wednesday that UK broker Gerrard Vivian Gray had agreed to resign as an AIM nominated adviser. No one at Gerard Vivian Gray was immediately available to comment.
The speculation follows a review of the performance of the 51 nominated advisors active in the market which caters to smaller companies.
The LSE confirmed it was "talking" with a "handful" of nominated advisors but declined to identify the brokers involved.
"We have not as of yet taken any disciplinary action against any adviser. Our investigations are still going on," the spokeswoman said.
The LSE said a nominated adviser which failed in its duties to monitor and advise companies it had brought to the market would normally face an initial private censure.
If the private censure failed, the broker would then face a public censure, where the adviser and its failings would be publicly criticised.
A total suspension from AIM would normally be the action of "last resort", the LSE said.
Brian Winterflood, chairman of an AIM nominated adviser Winterflood Securities believes the fledgling exchange's systems have performed well since its inception in June 1995.
"All you have to do is look at how many people have been turned down to be nominated advisors," Winterflood told Reuters.
Winterflood, who is a member of the AIM Advisory Committee which helps the LSE oversee the market, noted that around 50 percent of applicants had been refused nominated adviser status.
"We don't want just any Tom, Dick, or Harry coming along and raising money in this market," he said.
The current review is part of a continuing scrutiny by the Exchange of AIM, which has attracted 258 companies since its launch.
Unlike the main London share market, AIM advisers involved in promoting stocks have a key role in what is intended as a more lax regulatory structure.
"This market was never designed for widows and orphans. Caveat emptor(let the buyer beware) has always been the creed," Winterflood said.
Designed for start-up companies where the possibility of high gains counter the higher risk involved, the performance of some AIM stocks has nonetheless fallen short of some expectations.
Another nominated adviser, who wished to remain anonymous, said it was unlikely the LSE would publish the names of advisers it had censured.
"That would only happen in extreme circumstances. To do so otherwise would open up the Exchange to lawsuits. It is probably better to do it quietly," the adviser said.
--Dale Faulken, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
